title: Kafka Partition Calculation
subtitle: Quantitative formulas and broker limits for sizing topic partitions in production and interviews.
keyTakeaways: Partition count is determined by throughput bounds: `Partitions = max(Target Throughput / Producer Throughput, Target Throughput / Consumer Throughput)`.
Because an individual consumer instance can process at most one partition's throughput, consumer processing velocity is almost always the limiting factor.
Over-partitioning introduces severe broker penalties: memory buffer overhead, open file descriptor exhaustion, and longer leader election failovers.
architectureDiagram:
PARTITION SIZING CALCULATION WORKFLOW
Requirement: Target Peak Throughput = 100 MB/sec

1. Single Producer Node Throughput = ~25 MB/sec
   Producers needed: 100 MB/sec ÷ 25 MB/sec = 4 Partitions

2. Single Consumer Pod Throughput (Database writes) = ~5 MB/sec
   Consumers needed: 100 MB/sec ÷ 5 MB/sec = 20 Partitions

Sizing Verdict: Partitions = max(4, 20) = 20 Partitions minimum!
(Size to 24 partitions for headroom and clean 3/6-broker divisibility)

sections.heading: The Quantitative Throughput Sizing Formula
sections.body: Guessing partition counts in production leads to either under-provisioned bottlenecks or over-partitioned cluster instability. Use the standard sizing formula: `NumPartitions = max(Tp / P, Tp / C)`, where `Tp` is the target peak throughput, `P` is single-partition producer throughput, and `C` is single-partition consumer throughput.
bullets: Producer Throughput (`P`): Writing sequentially to a partition typically achieves 20 to 50 MB/sec per partition.
Consumer Throughput (`C`): Reading and executing database mutations or external RPCs is almost always the bottleneck, typically capping at 2 to 10 MB/sec per consumer thread.
Divisibility Rule: Always round partition counts to a multiple of your broker count (e.g., for a 6-broker cluster, choose 12, 18, or 24 partitions) so partitions distribute with perfect symmetry.

sections.heading: Why You Should Not Create 10,000 Partitions per Topic
sections.body: Engineers often ask: 'Why not just create 1,000 partitions upfront so we never have to re-partition?' Over-partitioning degrades broker stability in three critical ways.
bullets: Open File Descriptors: Each partition maintains multiple segment files (data log, offset index, timestamp index). 1,000 partitions require thousands of open OS file handles per broker.
Producer Memory Buffering: Producers allocate batch buffers per partition. 1,000 partitions inflate producer client RAM usage, causing garbage collection stalls.

Leader Election Latency: When a broker crashes, the cluster controller must elect new leaders for every partition that broker was leading. Having 10,000 partitions on a downed broker stretches failover time from milliseconds to tens of seconds.

tradeOffs.pros: Perfect balance of parallel consumer throughput; fast broker failover; compact memory footprint.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires increasing partition count and triggering consumer rebalances if traffic expands 10x.

tradeOffs.pros: Maximum theoretical consumer concurrency headroom without needing future topic alterations.
tradeOffs.cons: Slower broker reboot times; higher client memory allocation; risks cluster-wide controller stalls.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Hyperscale analytics ingestion on massive multi-hundred-broker clusters.

interviewTip: When sizing Kafka partitions in a system design interview, walk through the math out loud: 'If our peak ingestion throughput is 100 MB/sec, and each consumer worker processes 5 MB/sec due to database write constraints, we need at least `100 / 5 = 20` partitions. Across our 6-broker cluster, we will provision 24 partitions so each broker hosts exactly 4 partitions.'
